newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ROTEN LIFTS SWISS HOPES OF GOLD.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ROTEN LIFTS SWISS HOPES OF GOLD.

text.p: Karin Roten gave Switzerland a real chance of ending their gold medal drought at the Alpine skiing world championships on Wednesday by leading after the first leg of a floodlit women's slalom.
The Swiss team as a whole have not won a world title since 1993 and the women since 1991, when Vreni Schneider won the slalom and Chantal Bournissen the combined.
Roten, a giant slalom silver medallist in 1996, clocked 52.62 seconds down the Kandahar piste in a leg that ended with the top nine all within a second of her time.
Deborah Compagnoni, the overwhelming Italian favourite, delighted the crowd with a strong second place just 0.05 seconds behind Roten.
Only 0.18 seconds divided the leading six with any one of them in with an excellent chance of gold.
They included two Austrians -- Elfi Eder in third place 0.08 seconds behind Roten and Sabine Egger in sixth place.
The second leg will be in the reverse 15 order.
"I really found a good rhythm from the third gate down, said Roten. "The conditions were fine and not as icy or as difficult as I had feared. I could really attack."
She said the time differences were so tight that she dare not even think about a medal yet.
"It will be a big fight in the second leg," she said.

Austrian-born Claudia Riegler, who skis for New Zealand and has won three World Cup slaloms so far this season, was the first starter but was fifth 0.17 seconds down and said afterwards that the cold night air had not helped.
"I should have attacked a little more, maybe I had too much respect for the course," she said. "Because it's a night slalom the air is so cold and I was really fighting."

Defending champion Pernilla Wiberg of Sweden, who is concentrating more on the speed events at this championships after winning giant, slalom and combined golds in the past, made an error at the top of the piste and was in 10th place.
"I lost a bit of concentration and the hill is not steep enough to make up some speed," she said.
"But I know I can do it in the second run."
The double Olympic champion fared better than her compatriot Ylva Nowen who crashed within sight of the finish.
The biggest surprise of the night was Briton Emma Carrick-Anderson who came from the 41st starting place to finish the leg 14th fastest, 1.58 seconds behind Roten.

Swiss medal hope Sonja Nef, who led after the first leg of the slalom at the Sierra Nevada championships in Spain last year only to crash out in the second run, saw her championship nightmare continue when she hooked the second gate.
Conditions had deteriorated just before Nef set out, with temperatures dropping and light snow falling. By the time the later skiers went down, the snow was far heavier.
Nef won a World Cup slalom here last year, also run under floodlights, for her only career win to date but was third in a giant last month.
"Maybe I was trying too hard because I really like the course," she said, a smile replacing the tears of last year.
